title: Name and count your own virtual threads

blocks.text: Tools built for platform threads can miss virtual threads: the page's pitfall is `Thread.getAllStackTraces()`, which does not include them at all. The page's advice is to name virtual threads through a builder factory (`Thread.ofVirtual().name("order-processor-", 0).factory()`) and to watch them with tools that do see them. Here you build a small one yourself.

items: `new CountingFactory(prefix)`; `newThread(r)` returns an unstarted **virtual** thread named `prefix + n`, where `n` counts the threads made so far, from `0`.
`running()` is the number of **this** factory's threads whose task has started and not yet ended. A task that **throws** has ended too.

rows: while the three tasks are blocked
a thread whose task throws, after it ends

blocks.text: Threads start and end on many carriers at once, so keep the count thread-safe; the tests cannot force two updates to collide, so that is good practice rather than graded.

cases.says: running() counts the factory's threads whose task is in progress, and drops to 0 when they are done.
The factory makes virtual threads whose names start with the prefix.
The threads are named prefix0, prefix1, prefix2, ... in the order they are made.
A thread whose task throws is no longer counted once it ends.
A thread the factory made but nobody started is not counted as running.
Two factories keep separate counts: while one has three running tasks, the other's running() is 0.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves virtual threads out, so they are named through a builder factory and watched with tools that see them.
